# Iūpiter: the stories first, then the spelling

The marks in **Iūpiter** make the most sense standing next to the myths they have to carry. So the myths come first.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**Iovem Lapidem.** The most binding Roman oath was sworn per Iovem Lapidem — by Jupiter the Stone.  When the fetial priests concluded a treaty, the pater patratus held a flint from the god's altar and recited the archaic formula while striking a suckling pig dead: si sciens fallo, tum me Dispiter salva urbe arceque bonis eiciat, ut ego hunc porcum hic hodie feriam — 'if I knowingly deceive, then may Father Dis and Jupiter cast me from city and citadel with the loss of all good things, as I strike this pig today' (the rite survives in Livy's account of the Alba Longa treaty, 1. 24, and in Festus' gloss on lapis).

**The Borrowed Face.** In the triumph, the victorious general rode through the streets of Rome in Iūpiter's own regalia — the purple and gold, the four-horse chariot, the face painted red with minium, 'Jupiter's own colour,' like the terracotta of the god's Capitol statue (Pliny, Natural History 33. 111) — while a slave in the chariot held the crown and whispered respice post te; hominem te esse memento: 'look behind you; remember you are a man' (Tertullian, Apologeticum 33. 4).

**Opima Spolia.** The rarest honour in Rome belonged to Iūpiter Feretrius, whose little temple Romulus himself had vowed: the spolia opima, 'rich spoils,' the arms stripped when a Roman commander killed the enemy king in single combat.  It was won three times in seven centuries — by Romulus over Acron of Caenina (Livy 1. 10), by Aulus Cornelius Cossus in the fifth century BCE (Livy 4.

## And Here Is What the Spelling Preserves

The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form *iuppiter* cannot show:

- **u → ū** — Macron: long /uː/ (Iūpiter): how long the vowel is held.

A storyteller pronouncing the name would restore every one of them by instinct. The file only writes down what the voice already knows.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Iūpiter
- **ASCII form:** iuppiter
- **Meaning:** "'Sky-father' (from *Dyēu-pater)"
- **Domain of influence:** Sky, Thunder, Sovereignty
- **Pantheon:** Roman
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** IVPPITER
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 241 of 546

## The Name Travels

Everywhere Rome went, Iūpiter wore local faces.  In the Greek East he was simply Zeús; at Siwa he was Ammon, the ram-horned father Alexander claimed as his own; in North Africa he absorbed the Carthaginian Baʿal Ḥammon as Iuppiter Ammon; on the Rhine frontier his columns show him riding down giants beside a wheel-bearing Taranis; and in the legionary forts from Britain to the Danube he was Dolichenus — a storm god in iron scale-armour standing on a bull.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Iūpiter** stands at [/iuppiter/](/iuppiter/) — [lore](/iuppiter/lore/), [scholars](/iuppiter/scholars/), [patterns](/iuppiter/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can express — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it, mechanically, in Tier-1.
